subject: security
title: Systems Security
summary: Memory-safety bugs and layered defences: what each mitigation can protect, its requirements and its limits.

lessons.title: Memory-safety bugs
lessons.summary: Buffer overflows, out-of-bounds reads, use-after-free, double free, integer overflows and format strings, why they are dangerous and how to fix and find them.
lessons.body:
C and C++ provide pointer operations without universal run-time bounds or lifetime checks. Accessing an object outside its bounds or lifetime can cause **undefined behaviour**: the language does not promise a clean crash, a particular overwrite, or access to arbitrary addresses. Operating-system mappings and permissions still constrain hardware accesses. The C examples below use the C11/C17 model.

These bugs can expose secrets or alter decisions as well as crash programs. Chromium reports that memory unsafety accounted for around 70% of a sample of 912 high/critical Stable-channel security bugs since 2015. This is a historical, project-specific sample, not a current universal percentage.

## Why a bug becomes a vulnerability

The diagram is an illustrative conventional process layout, not a C requirement (addresses increase upwards). Real systems may use multiple heap mappings; stack direction, saved registers and return-address storage depend on the architecture and compiler.

```
high  +------------------------+
      | stack (grows down)     |
      |  locals, saved regs,   |
      |  return addresses      |
      +------------------------+
      |         ...            |
      +------------------------+
      | heap (grows up)        |
      |  malloc'd objects and  |
      |  allocator metadata    |
      +------------------------+
      | globals, .data, .bss   |
      | program code (.text)   |
low   +------------------------+
```

The security concern is proximity: a buffer can share an allocation or stack frame with sensitive data. Depending on the implementation, nearby data can include control pointers or allocator metadata. Corrupting an authorization flag can also compromise a program without hijacking control flow.

So a bug that writes past the end of a buffer does not just corrupt "some data". It can overwrite something that decides **what the program does next**. That is the step from crash to compromise, and it is why the defences in the next lesson focus on protecting that control data.

Two important families are spatial and temporal errors. This classification does not describe every issue below; uninitialised-value use also needs separate attention.

| Family | Question it breaks | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Spatial | Is this address inside the object? | Overflow, OOB read |
| Temporal | Is the object still alive? | Use-after-free, double free |

## Stack buffer overflow

The classic bug is copying input into a fixed-size buffer without checking its length.

```c
void greet(const char *name) {
    char buf[16];
    strcpy(buf, name);   /* BUG */
    printf("Hello, %s\n", buf);
}
```

`strcpy` requires enough destination space for all source bytes and the terminating NUL. A valid 40-byte name needs 41 bytes, exceeding `buf` by 25. Calling it here violates that requirement; a neighbouring-data overwrite is one possible outcome, not a guaranteed execution trace. Include `<string.h>` and `<stdio.h>` when compiling these function fragments.

The fix is to pass the destination size and handle truncation deliberately:

```c
void greet(const char *name) {
    char buf[16];
    int n = snprintf(buf, sizeof buf,
                     "%s", name);
    if (n < 0 || (size_t)n >= sizeof buf) {
        /* too long: reject or log */
        return;
    }
    printf("Hello, %s\n", buf);
}
```

With valid, non-overlapping arguments, `snprintf` bounds output by the supplied capacity and terminates it when that capacity is non-zero. Its non-negative return reports the required length excluding NUL; a negative return reports an error. The example rejects both errors and truncation. The source must itself be a valid NUL-terminated string.

> [!warning] strncpy is not a safe strcpy
> `strncpy(dst, src, n)` stops at `n` bytes, but if `src` is `n` bytes or longer it does **not** write a terminating NUL. An unbounded string operation on that unterminated destination violates its input requirements and can read past the end. Prefer `snprintf`, or `strlcpy` where available.

### Off-by-one errors

Many overflows are a single element too far:

```c
char id[8];
for (int i = 0; i <= 8; i++)  /* BUG */
    id[i] = src[i];
```

With a source of at least nine bytes, the faulty loop attempts indices 0 through 8. For an eight-byte raw copy, use `i < 8` and a source of at least eight bytes. That correction does not create a NUL-terminated string: reserve and write a terminator if string APIs will consume the result.

## Out-of-bounds reads: Heartbleed

Reading beyond an object can disclose memory if the result becomes observable. It may instead fault or have other undefined behaviour. Potential disclosures include secrets and addresses that weaken ASLR.

**Heartbleed** (CVE-2014-0160) in OpenSSL is the famous case. The TLS heartbeat message said "here are N bytes, echo them back". OpenSSL trusted the attacker-supplied N without checking it against how much data had actually arrived. Simplified:

```c
/* len comes from the packet */
memcpy(reply, payload, len);  /* BUG */
```

A malformed request could make vulnerable OpenSSL disclose up to 64 KB of process memory, potentially including secrets. A crash or other outcome was also possible. For a TLS heartbeat model, first ensure the three-byte header exists before parsing its length; reserve the required minimum 16-byte padding too. With non-negative `size_t` lengths and a sufficiently large reply buffer, the following guard prevents subtraction underflow:

```c
if (record_len < 3 + 16)
    return 0;
if (len > record_len - 3 - 16)
    return 0;  /* discard bad message */
memcpy(reply, payload, len);
```

Treat externally supplied lengths, indices and counts as untrusted. Validate both the arithmetic and the resulting range against actual available storage before parsing or copying.

## Integer overflow leading to a small allocation

Size arithmetic can wrap around. Consider:

```c
/* count comes from a file header */
item *arr = malloc(count * sizeof(item));
for (uint32_t i = 0; i < count; i++)
    read_item(&arr[i]);
```

Assume both `count` and `size_t` are 32-bit unsigned types, and `sizeof(item)` is 16. Then `0x10000001 * 16 = 0x100000010` wraps to `0x10`: only 16 bytes are requested. Allocation may fail; if it succeeds, attempting all those item writes exceeds the allocation and invokes undefined behaviour.

Fixes:

- Check before multiplying: `if (count > SIZE_MAX / sizeof(item)) fail;`
- On documented implementations such as glibc, `calloc(count, sizeof(item))` and `reallocarray` reject size overflow. `reallocarray` is POSIX, not ISO C. Check allocation failure before dereferencing; define a policy for zero counts.
- Reject absurd values early: a sane upper bound on `count` is good input validation anyway.

## Use-after-free

A **use-after-free** (UAF) is a temporal bug: the program keeps using a pointer after the memory it points to has been released.

```c
struct session *s = load_session();
if (expired(s))
    free(s);
/* ... later, on another path ... */
if (s->is_admin)   /* BUG: s may be freed */
    grant_access();
```

An allocator may reuse freed storage for a later allocation. If request-controlled bytes occupy that storage, a dangling access can influence an authorization decision or a control pointer. Reuse timing is allocator-dependent, and undefined behaviour means no particular result is guaranteed. The fragment assumes `load_session` succeeded; real code must also handle failure.

Defences in C:

- After `free`, setting an owning pointer to `NULL` can support later explicit null checks and makes `free(NULL)` harmless. Dereferencing NULL is still undefined behaviour, not a guaranteed clean crash; other aliases still dangle.
- Give every allocation **one clear owner** responsible for freeing it, and document which functions borrow versus take ownership.
- In C++, prefer `std::unique_ptr` for exclusive ownership, using `std::shared_ptr` when ownership really is shared. Raw borrowed aliases and unsynchronised access still require lifetime discipline.

### Double free

Freeing the same allocation twice is undefined behaviour; `free(NULL)` is exempt. Outcomes can include allocator corruption or a diagnostic abort. Detection is implementation-dependent and does not make double free safe. Clear ownership and avoiding stale aliases prevent the underlying error.

## Format-string bugs

```c
printf(user_input);          /* BUG */
printf("%s", user_input);    /* fixed */
```

An untrusted format can request conversions such as `%x` or `%n`. Missing or incorrectly typed arguments invoke undefined behaviour; depending on the calling convention and program, this can expose values or attempt a memory write. `%n` stores a character count through its supplied pointer. Use a fixed format and valid string argument. GCC/Clang warnings such as `-Wformat -Wformat-security -Werror=format-security` reject the illustrated no-extra-arguments mistake.

## Uninitialised memory

An uninitialised automatic value is indeterminate in C11/C17, and many uses have undefined behaviour. Do not assume it reliably returns old bytes. Separately, copying a raw structure across a trust boundary can disclose padding. Initialising members with `{0}` is not a portable guarantee that padding remains zero after member stores. Encode named fields into an explicitly defined byte representation instead of transmitting `sizeof(struct)` bytes.

## Finding these bugs

You will not find memory bugs reliably by reading code alone. The standard toolkit:

| Tool | How it works | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| AddressSanitizer | Instrumented accesses checked against shadow memory | Workload-dependent |
| Valgrind Memcheck | Dynamic binary instrumentation | Workload-dependent |
| Fuzzing | Generates varied test inputs | Depends on budget |
| Static analysis | Reasons about code without running it | False positives |

**AddressSanitizer** (`-fsanitize=address` in Clang/GCC) uses poisoned regions and delayed reuse to detect many invalid accesses. It can report errors such as `heap-use-after-free`. Coverage depends on instrumentation, allocation layout and execution: it does not check every object boundary, every uninitialised value or every possible input. Intra-object overwrites and accesses after storage is reused may escape detection.

**Fuzzers** such as libFuzzer and AFL++ use feedback to explore inputs. Combining fuzzing with sanitizers helps expose faults on executed paths; neither proves absence of bugs. OSS-Fuzz provides continuous fuzzing for eligible open-source projects. Valid regression tests remain useful alongside malformed-input tests.

> [!tip] A C/C++ testing baseline
> Enable useful warnings, test with ASan/UBSan where supported, and fuzz untrusted-input parsers. Review unbounded string operations; `gets` was removed from C11. A clean sanitizer run is evidence about those executions, not proof of memory safety.

> [!note] Content omitted after review
> A universal current vulnerability percentage, a ranking of the most productive testing technique, and fixed sanitizer costs are omitted because this review did not establish representative measurements. Historical Chromium figures describe only its stated sample.

## Key takeaways
- Spatial and temporal errors are important families; uninitialised-value bugs also need attention.
- They are dangerous because data and control information share memory, so corruption can redirect execution.
- Invalid reads can disclose secrets, invalid writes can corrupt state, and stale aliases can expose reused storage; outcomes are not guaranteed.
- Every externally supplied length, index or count must be checked against the real buffer size, including the arithmetic that computes it.
- Find bugs with sanitizers and fuzzing, not just review, and prevent them with bounded APIs and clear ownership.

## Further reading
- [C11 committee draft, object/lifetime and library rules](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf)
- [Heartbleed advisory — OpenSSL](https://openssl-library.org/news/secadv/20140407.txt)
- [TLS heartbeat format — RFC 6520](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6520.html)
- [CWE-416: Use After Free — MITRE](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/416.html)
- [The Heartbleed Bug](https://heartbleed.com/)
- [AddressSanitizer — Clang documentation](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AddressSanitizer.html)
- [Memory safety — Chromium security](https://www.chromium.org/Home/chromium-security/memory-safety/)
- [OSS-Fuzz — Google](https://google.github.io/oss-fuzz/)

options.text: 10 bytes required, exceeding capacity by 2
options.explanation: This forgets the NUL terminator. `strcpy` copies the string's characters *and* the terminating `\0`.

options.text: 8 bytes required, fitting exactly
options.explanation: The required destination capacity includes the entire source and its NUL. The API has no destination-capacity argument.

options.text: 11 bytes required, exceeding capacity by 3
options.explanation: Ten single-byte letters plus NUL require 11 bytes; capacity is 8. This does not guarantee any particular overwrite when the invalid call executes.

options.text: It fails to compile because the string is too long
options.explanation: A diagnostic may be issued or treated as a build error. The C language does not require a compiler to reject this library-precondition violation.

questions.workedExample: The required capacity is 10 + 1 = 11 bytes, exceeding 8 by 3. The call is invalid; it might corrupt neighbouring state, abort or behave otherwise. Use a bounded API with valid arguments and check truncation/errors.

options.explanation: Classic off-by-one: this runs for i = 0..8, nine iterations, and writes `id[8]`, which is one past the end.
Correct. Valid indices for an 8-element array are 0 to 7; `i < 8` stops after writing index 7.

options.text: `i <= sizeof id`
options.explanation: `sizeof id` is 8, so this is the same off-by-one as `i <= 8`.
Equivalent to `i <= 8`: nine iterations, the last writing out of bounds.

questions.workedExample: For an eight-byte raw copy with at least eight readable source bytes, `i < 8` visits indices 0 through 7. Conditions allowing index 8 overrun the destination. This raw copy does not guarantee a NUL terminator; a string needs room for one and an explicit termination policy.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a **temporal** memory-safety bug rather than a spatial one?

options.text: Writing `arr[10]` into a 10-element array
options.explanation: That is spatial: the address is outside the object's bounds, even though the object is alive.

options.text: Heartbleed's over-long `memcpy` read
options.explanation: Also spatial: an out-of-bounds read past the end of a live buffer.

options.text: Reading `s->name` after `free(s)`
options.explanation: Correct. The address was once valid, but the object's lifetime has ended. That is a use-after-free, a temporal bug.

options.text: A `malloc` size that wrapped round to a small number
options.explanation: Wrapping can produce an undersized request; later accesses beyond the actual allocation are spatial errors. The arithmetic alone is not a temporal error.

questions.workedExample: Spatial checks concern object boundaries; temporal checks concern lifetime. In the selected option the session has been freed, so accessing its former member is invalid even though that member belonged to the original layout. A wrapped allocation can lead to spatial errors when code later exceeds the actual allocation.

options.text: `11 [hello world]`
options.explanation: `snprintf` never writes more than `sizeof d` bytes, so the full string cannot be stored in an 8-byte buffer.

options.text: `7 [hello w]`
options.explanation: The contents are right but the return value is not the number of characters written; it is the length the full output *would* have had.

options.text: `11 [hello w]`
options.explanation: Correct. It stores 7 characters plus a NUL in the 8 bytes, and returns 11, the untruncated length. `n >= sizeof d` tells you it truncated.

options.text: `-1 [hello w]`
options.explanation: A negative return means an encoding error, not truncation. C99 `snprintf` returns the would-be length on truncation.

questions.prompt: A reviewer replaces `strcpy(dst, src)` with `strncpy(dst, src, sizeof dst)` where `dst` is `char dst[4]` and `src` is `"abcdef"`. What is the remaining problem?

options.text: None; `strncpy` is the safe version of `strcpy`
options.explanation: This is the common misconception. `strncpy` bounds the write but does not guarantee a terminator.

options.text: `strncpy` still writes 7 bytes
options.explanation: It writes at most `n` = 4 bytes, so there is no write overflow here.

options.text: `dst` has no NUL terminator, so unbounded string operations on it are invalid
options.explanation: The four bytes are `abcd`, with no terminator. Passing that array to an unbounded string operation violates its input requirements and can over-read.

options.text: `strncpy` pads with spaces, corrupting the string
options.explanation: It pads with NUL bytes, and only when the source is *shorter* than `n`.

questions.workedExample: Four source bytes fill `dst` as `abcd`; no NUL fits. An unbounded string operation is invalid on this result. Use a bounded formatting/copy API with error and truncation checks, or explicitly terminate within the destination while treating lost data as truncation. `strlcpy` is an option only where provided.

questions.prompt:
Assume `size_t` and `count` are 32-bit unsigned types, `count = 0x10000001`, and an item needs 16 bytes. What byte count is passed to `malloc`? Allocation success is not assumed.

```c
item *a = malloc(count * 16);
```

options.text: 16 bytes requested
options.explanation: The mathematical product is 0x100000010. Reduced modulo 2^32 it is 0x10, or 16; attempting all intended item writes would exceed a successful allocation.

options.text: About 4 GB
options.explanation: The true product is about 4 GB, but it cannot be represented in a 32-bit `size_t`, so it wraps.

options.text: 0 bytes, and malloc returns NULL
options.explanation: The wrapped value is 0x10, not 0. Only the bits above bit 31 are lost.

options.text: The multiplication traps and the program aborts
options.explanation: Unsigned arithmetic in C wraps silently modulo 2^32; there is no trap unless you add a check or a sanitizer.

questions.workedExample: 0x10000001 * 16 = 0x100000010; modulo 2^32 gives 16. Check `count > SIZE_MAX / sizeof(item)` before multiplication, apply an application limit, and handle allocation failure. On implementations such as glibc, `calloc(count, sizeof(item))` rejects multiplication overflow, but its return must still be checked.

questions.prompt: For valid NUL-terminated `msg`, which changes fix the illustrated format-string flaw in `printf(msg);`, or reject it at build time with GCC/Clang? Select all that apply.

options.text: Change it to `printf("%s", msg);`
options.explanation: Correct. The format string is now a constant, and the user's text is only ever data printed by `%s`.

options.text: Use `fputs(msg, stdout);`
options.explanation: Correct. `fputs` does not interpret format directives at all, so `%n` and `%x` are just characters.

options.text: Compile with `-Wformat -Wformat-security -Werror`
options.explanation: Correct as prevention: the compiler flags non-literal format strings with no arguments and the build fails until it is fixed.

options.text: Strip newline characters from `msg`
options.explanation: Newlines are harmless here. The dangerous characters are `%` directives, and filtering is a fragile substitute for the real fix.

options.text: Make `msg` a larger buffer
options.explanation: Buffer size is irrelevant: the bug is that user data is interpreted as instructions to `printf`.

questions.workedExample: Untrusted text controls the conversion directives. Missing or wrongly typed arguments cause undefined behaviour and can expose data or attempt writes; their locations depend on the calling convention. A fixed `%s` format or `fputs` treats the valid string as data. The listed warning/error flags reject this specific no-extra-arguments pattern, not every possible misuse.

questions.prompt: A malformed Heartbleed request supplied fewer payload bytes than its length field claimed. Which behaviour made the vulnerable OpenSSL implementation an information-disclosure vulnerability?

options.text: Crashed immediately on the oversized length
options.explanation: A crash was possible, but was not a reliable protection. The vulnerability could disclose process memory rather than rejecting every malformed request.

options.text: It could copy beyond the supplied payload into a response, disclosing up to about 64 KB
options.explanation: Correct. `memcpy` used the attacker's length without checking it against the record's real size, so it over-read adjacent heap memory, which could hold keys and cookies.

options.text: Wrote 64 KB of attacker data over its heap
options.explanation: Heartbleed was an out-of-bounds *read* (an information leak), not a write.

options.text: Rejected the message because TLS records are authenticated
options.explanation: The heartbeat was processed inside the TLS layer; record authentication does not validate this inner length field.

questions.workedExample: The request contains a type, two-byte payload length, payload and at least 16 padding bytes. Vulnerable code trusted the claimed length in a copy. A robust parser first checks that the header is present, parses the length, and then checks payload plus minimum padding against the remaining record. The review does not assume every malformed maximum-length request yields an identical complete reply.

questions.prompt: A server frees a `session` object on logout but a cached pointer to it survives. Shortly after, a request allocates a buffer of the same size and fills it with request data. Why is the later `if (sess->is_admin)` check dangerous rather than merely buggy?

options.text: Because freed memory is zeroed, so `is_admin` reads as false and locks users out
options.explanation: Freeing storage does not promise that a later invalid access reads zero. Denying legitimate access can itself be a security/availability problem.

options.text: The allocator may reuse that storage for request data, allowing a stale access to influence authorization
options.explanation: If reuse occurs, the stale access can observe storage occupied by request-controlled bytes. The access is undefined behaviour, so this is a threat scenario rather than a promised C execution trace.

options.text: Because `free` returns the page to the OS, so access always segfaults
options.explanation: The allocator may retain the mapping or release it; neither behaviour makes stale access valid or guarantees a segmentation fault.

options.text: Because the compiler removes the check after `free`
options.explanation: The compiler has no obligation to preserve a meaningful check after undefined behaviour. Optimisation is another reason the result cannot be predicted; allocation reuse explains the illustrated security risk.

questions.workedExample: A possible sequence is allocate X, free X, reuse X for request bytes, then access X through a stale alias. Prevent it through ownership and lifetime discipline. Nulling one pointer does not invalidate all aliases. ASan can detect accesses while freed storage remains poisoned, but may miss accesses after that address has been reused for a live allocation.

questions.prompt: You maintain a C image decoder that parses untrusted files. Which practices give the best chance of finding memory-safety bugs **before** release? Select all that apply.

options.text: Coverage-guided fuzzing (libFuzzer or AFL++) of the decode function
options.explanation: Coverage-guided fuzzing explores varied inputs and paths within the available budget; it has no universal minimum input count or productivity ranking.

options.text: Running the fuzzer and tests with AddressSanitizer enabled
options.explanation: ASan detects many invalid accesses on executed instrumented paths. Instrumentation gaps, same-object overwrites and reused live storage can escape detection.

options.text: Testing only with a corpus of valid sample images
options.explanation: Valid-image tests are useful, and valid inputs can reveal bugs too. Using only them leaves important malformed-input and error-handling paths untested.

options.text: Shipping with `-O3` so the code runs faster
options.explanation: Higher optimisation is not a replacement for tests or detectors; it can change how undefined behaviour manifests.

options.text: Joining OSS-Fuzz or running fuzzing continuously in CI
options.explanation: Continuous fuzzing can expose newly introduced failures within its input and instrumentation coverage. OSS-Fuzz has project eligibility requirements.

questions.workedExample: Combine valid regression cases, malformed-input fuzzing, sanitizer-enabled runs and continuous retesting. Results depend on exercised paths and detector coverage. Optimisation alone is not a bug-finding strategy, and a clean run does not prove safety.

options.text: None; both fields are initialised
options.explanation: The members are assigned, but that does not establish safe portable contents for the padding bytes.

options.text: `sizeof r` is 9, so the copy is too short
options.explanation: With 8-byte alignment for `uint64_t`, the struct is 16 bytes, not 9.

options.text: Seven padding bytes may contain unspecified data and disclose information
options.explanation: Under the stated ABI offsets 1 through 7 are padding. Assigning members does not establish portable padding contents, so serializing the raw object can disclose unintended bytes.

options.text: `uint8_t` cannot be copied to user space
options.explanation: Any bytes can be copied; the problem is which bytes are in the struct.

questions.workedExample: Given the stated layout, flag uses byte 0, padding occupies bytes 1–7, and value uses bytes 8–15. Do not transmit the padding. Encode the two named fields into an explicit wire format with defined endianness. `{0}` or an earlier `memset` is not a portable guarantee that padding stays zero after later member stores.

lessons.title: Exploit mitigations
lessons.summary: Stack canaries, DEP/NX, ASLR, RELRO, FORTIFY_SOURCE, control-flow integrity, shadow stacks and memory tagging, what each one stops and what it doesn't.
lessons.body:
Memory-unsafe operations can leave exploitable bugs in a program. Compilers, operating systems and CPUs provide **mitigations** that restrict particular ways of exploiting them. Their effectiveness depends on the enabled features and the program.

A mitigation does not repair the faulty source operation. It may prevent exploitation or terminate the process, but a crash is still an availability/security failure. A program may also leak information or corrupt sensitive data before a check fires. Some attacks need several vulnerabilities; there is no universal minimum chain length.

## The attacker's checklist

A classic control-flow attack may corrupt a return address or function pointer, determine a useful destination and redirect execution there. Other attacks change data, such as an authorization flag, without these steps.

The mitigations below address different parts of that process. None covers every possible memory-safety failure.

## Stack canaries

A **stack canary** is a guard value checked by compiler-generated code on protected function exits. A common downward-growing stack layout places it between buffers and the saved return address, as illustrated below; exact layout and coverage depend on the ABI, compiler and optimisation.

```
higher addresses
+---------------------+
| return address      |
| saved frame pointer |
| CANARY (random)     |  <- checked at exit
| char buf[64]        |  <- overflow goes up
| other locals        |
+---------------------+
lower addresses
```

A linear overflow from `buf` must pass through the canary to reach the return address. If the value has changed, the program calls `__stack_chk_fail` and aborts instead of returning.

Details that matter:

- In the inspected glibc implementation, startup randomness initializes the guard and its first byte in memory is cleared. On little-endian x86-64 this is the lowest byte. A NUL-terminated copy cannot both preserve that byte and continue past it; the destination NUL does **not** itself stop an overflowing copy.
- GCC `-fstack-protector-strong` covers local arrays and references to local frame addresses, considering variables that actually remain on the stack after optimisation.
- Do not rely on a universal ordering of other locals or assume every function is protected.

What canaries don't stop: heap overflows, overwrites of other data *before* the function returns (such as a function pointer used inside it), overflows within a struct (field order is fixed by the language), and attacks where a separate bug leaks the canary's value first.

## DEP / NX: data is not code

**DEP/NX** prevents instruction execution from pages marked non-executable. Write and execute permissions are separate: NX alone does not enforce **W^X**, the stronger policy that a page must not be writable and executable simultaneously. The table illustrates common permissions, not a guarantee for every mapping.

| Region | Read | Write | Execute |
|---|---|---|---|
| Code (.text) | yes | no | yes |
| Stack | yes | yes | no |
| Heap | yes | yes | no |

An attempt to fetch instructions from a non-executable stack or heap page faults. Whether the process then terminates depends on OS handling. A process can have executable mappings, including generated code; enabling DEP does not mean every data allocation is necessarily non-executable.

Attackers responded with **code-reuse** attacks: rather than injecting new code, they redirect control through short snippets of code that already exist in the program and its libraries, which are legitimately executable. The best-known form is **return-oriented programming** (ROP). Code reuse is why DEP alone is not enough, and why the attacker's "know where" step became so important.

JIT compilers generate executable code at run time. Their permission transitions and aliases need careful protection; a writable alias of executable storage can undermine the intended restriction. The exact mechanism is platform-specific.

## ASLR: hide the addresses

**Address space layout randomisation** varies placement of selected mappings, such as libraries and stacks, when a process image is loaded. Support and configuration determine which mappings vary. A fork normally inherits the existing address space. Wrong target guesses can fail or crash; neither outcome is guaranteed for every corruption.

How much it helps depends on **entropy**, the number of random bits:

- With eight independent uniformly random bits, there are `2^8 = 256` possibilities.
- With 28 such bits, there are `2^28 = 268,435,456` possibilities.

These are teaching examples, not asserted Linux defaults. Architecture, kernel settings and distribution policy affect actual entropy. On supported Linux systems, `vm.mmap_rnd_bits` controls randomisation for relevant mappings.

Two caveats make ASLR weaker than the numbers suggest:

1. **Leaks can weaken ASLR.** A pointer into a known library build at a known offset reveals that mapping base. It does not automatically reveal unrelated mappings or unknown builds.
2. **Coverage matters.** Conventional non-PIE ELF executables have fixed main-code addresses. PIE permits random placement when the loader and OS enable it; compiler flags alone are not proof of effective randomisation.

Linux can randomise its kernel base when **KASLR** is supported and enabled. A known-offset kernel pointer leak can weaken that protection.

## RELRO and FORTIFY_SOURCE

Two more toolchain hardening features are common on Linux:

- **RELRO** makes a designated ELF relocation region read-only after relocation. In a conventional supported ELF toolchain, full RELRO (`-Wl,-z,relro,-z,now`) also resolves lazy function bindings at load time so the GOT can be protected. Later `dlopen` loads have their own relocations. This does not protect every function pointer in a program.
- **`_FORTIFY_SOURCE`** adds compile-time diagnostics and run-time checks to supported library calls where object-size information is available. Level 3 uses dynamic object-size information and requires a compatible compiler/libc; glibc enables these wrappers only with optimisation. Unknown sizes and unsupported operations can remain unchecked.

An illustrative GNU/Linux ELF build fragment follows. It requires toolchain support for level-3 fortification; the CET-related flag is for supported x86 targets. Check platform documentation and the resulting binary/runtime configuration. Accepting a flag does not prove that hardware enforcement is active.

```
CFLAGS += -O2 -fstack-protector-strong \
  -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3 -fPIE \
  -fcf-protection=full
LDFLAGS += -pie -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now
```

## Control-flow integrity

**Control-flow integrity** constrains allowed control transfers. Different schemes cover different indirect calls, jumps or returns; they do not all check every transfer or enforce the same policy.

### Forward edges: indirect calls

An indirect call (`fp()`, a C++ virtual call) should only reach functions that could validly be called there.

- **Clang CFI** includes type-based indirect-call and virtual-call checks. Its `-fsanitize=cfi` family requires the documented LTO/visibility setup; a flag alone is not a complete build recipe.
- **Microsoft CFG** validates instrumented indirect calls against allowed targets; it is not a complete type-based policy.
- **Intel IBT** and **Arm BTI** constrain relevant indirect branches to suitable landing pads when enforcement is enabled. Landing-pad validation is coarser than checking the intended function type.

### Backward edges: returns

A **shadow stack** keeps protected return-address copies. With x86 CET shadow-stack enforcement, calls update the two stacks and returns check agreement. Linux user-space use requires supporting CPU, kernel, runtime and enablement; kernel availability alone does not protect every application.

**Pointer authentication** can protect selected Arm pointers with a keyed authentication code, incorporating contextual information. It authenticates rather than encrypts the pointer, and is not a general memory-safety check. Code generation, authentication policy and hardware support determine coverage.

The permitted-target set depends on the CFI policy. Type-based schemes may still permit an unintended same-type target; landing-pad schemes can permit a broader set. Shadow stacks protect returns by a different check, so a same-type target is not itself a shadow-stack bypass.

## Memory tagging

**Arm MTE** associates four-bit allocation tags with 16-byte granules of suitably configured memory and compares them with pointer tags on checked accesses. Software must arrange tagging and retagging; hardware does not infer every object lifetime. Under an explicitly uniform independent choice among all 16 tags, a stale tag matches with probability `1/16`. Actual allocator policies, unchecked accesses and same-granule overflows change coverage. In synchronous mode a mismatch is reported at the access; asynchronous mode can allow execution to continue before reporting.

Allocator hardening also narrows some failure modes. glibc safe-linking encodes selected singly linked free-list pointers; it does not prevent all heap corruption. Chrome BackupRefPtr, one MiraclePtr implementation, quarantines eligible allocations while tracked `raw_ptr` references remain. Untracked raw aliases and unsupported allocations are outside that guarantee.

## Summary table

| Mitigation | Breaks | Typical bypass |
|---|---|---|
| Canary | Return overwrite | Leak, non-linear write |
| DEP/NX | Injected code | Code reuse |
| ASLR | Known addresses | Info leak |
| Full RELRO | GOT overwrite | Other pointers |
| Type-based forward CFI | Invalid indirect-call targets | Unintended allowed target |
| Shadow stack | Forged returns | Outside coverage or disabled enforcement |
| MTE | Some invalid tagged accesses | Tag match or unchecked boundary |

> [!note] Defence in depth
> Combine protections and fix the source bug. Data-only corruption, information disclosure and failures outside enabled coverage remain possible. Extra vulnerabilities are sometimes needed for exploitation, but a mitigation does not force every attacker to find another bug.

> [!note] Content omitted after review
> Universal ASLR defaults, platform-wide deployment rates, fixed exploit costs and guaranteed crash or prevention rates are omitted because this review did not establish the necessary versioned measurements. MTE and CET hardware enforcement were not exercised in this review.

## Key takeaways
- Mitigations restrict specific exploitation paths; they do not fix bugs or guarantee a safe outcome.
- Enabled canary checks detect some return-address overwrites; NX blocks execution from non-executable pages; ASLR varies selected mapping bases.
- Existing executable code can evade NX; a known-offset pointer leak can weaken ASLR for that mapping.
- CFI and shadow stacks constrain where indirect calls and returns can go; MTE catches many bad accesses directly.
- Use hardening supported by the target platform and verify both binary properties and runtime enablement.

questions.prompt: Assume a corrupted return transfers execution to injected bytes on a stack page explicitly marked non-executable, and no earlier protection stops it. What does DEP/NX enforce?

options.text: The injected instructions run with the process's privileges
options.explanation: This is what happened before NX. With NX the stack is not executable, so the CPU refuses to fetch instructions from it.

options.text: Instruction fetch from that page faults; normal OS handling may terminate the process
options.explanation: NX rejects instruction fetch from a non-executable page. W^X is a separate stronger policy forbidding simultaneous write and execute permissions.

options.text: ASLR moves the bytes elsewhere so they run safely
options.explanation: ASLR randomises where regions are loaded; it does not relocate or sanitise data at run time.

options.text: The canary check prevents the return entirely
options.explanation: A canary might stop some overwrites earlier, but the scenario explicitly assumes the transfer reaches the non-executable page.

questions.workedExample: The page is explicitly non-executable. Fetching an instruction there faults even though it contains valid machine-code bytes. NX does not forbid ordinary writes, and it alone does not forbid writable/executable mappings elsewhere. Existing executable code is outside this particular prohibition.

questions.prompt: In the conventional protected stack-frame layout shown in the lesson, where is the canary and when is it checked?

options.text: At the very bottom of the stack, checked when the program exits
options.explanation: A per-process check at exit would be far too late: the hijacked return would already have happened.

options.text: Between the local buffers and the saved return address, checked just before the function returns
options.explanation: Correct. A linear overflow from a buffer must cross the canary to reach the return address, and the epilogue verifies it before `ret`.

options.text: Inside every heap allocation, checked on `free`
options.explanation: That describes some heap hardening, not stack canaries. Canaries protect stack frames.

options.text: In the CPU's shadow stack, checked on every instruction
options.explanation: Shadow stacks are a separate hardware mechanism and hold copies of return addresses, not canaries.

questions.workedExample: Picture the frame from high to low addresses: return address, saved frame pointer, **canary**, buffers. An overflow writes upward from a buffer, so it hits the canary before it can reach the return address. The function's epilogue compares the canary with the per-process secret and calls `__stack_chk_fail` if they differ, so the corrupted return address is never used.

questions.prompt: What is ASLR's main contribution to stopping exploitation?

options.text: It encrypts memory so stolen bytes are useless
options.explanation: ASLR does not encrypt anything; memory contents are unchanged, only their location varies.

options.text: It makes selected mapping addresses harder to predict without additional information
options.explanation: Random placement makes a useful target harder to predict. Effectiveness depends on entropy, leaks and other context; failure or a crash is possible rather than guaranteed.

options.text: It prevents buffer overflows from happening
options.explanation: ASLR does nothing to stop the overflow itself; it makes using it harder.

options.text: It stops the CPU executing data pages
options.explanation: That is NX/DEP, a different mitigation.

questions.workedExample: ASLR varies selected mapping bases under the OS policy. A known-offset leak can reveal a mapping base; a fork may inherit it. With no useful disclosure, an attacker may need to guess. Incorrect guesses can fail or crash, but ASLR does not stop all pointer corruption or data-only attacks.

options.text: The canary detects the overflow and the program aborts before `grant()`
options.explanation: A canary may be checked only at a protected exit, after the authorization decision. It does not bounds-check the member copy.

options.text: The compiler reorders `name` after `is_admin`, so the overflow is harmless
options.explanation: Compilers can reorder separate local variables, but C fixes the order of fields inside a struct, so `is_admin` must follow `name`.

options.text: The overflow can corrupt `is_admin`, which is used before an exit-time canary check
options.explanation: A neighbouring data field can affect authorization before the function exits. The exact outcome is undefined, and a canary is not a general check of every local value.

options.text: DEP stops the write because the stack is non-executable
options.explanation: NX controls execution, not writes. The stack is writable by design.

questions.workedExample: Under the stated ABI the flag follows the 16-byte name array. An overlong copy can affect the flag, and the decision occurs before the normal exit check. This is a possible data-corruption risk, not a guaranteed C execution. Fix the invalid copy and validate truncation/errors rather than relying on a guard.

questions.prompt: A teaching model has 256 equally likely library bases (eight bits of entropy). Forked workers keep the same unknown base after crashes. Each wrong guess crashes a worker. Trying each candidate at most once, approximately how many attempts are needed on average?

options.text: About 8
options.explanation: 8 is the number of *bits*, not the number of possibilities. Each bit doubles the search space.

options.text: About 128
options.explanation: For 256 equally likely fixed bases, trying each candidate once gives expected position (256 + 1)/2 = 128.5, approximately 128. Elapsed time is not specified.

options.text: About 268 million
options.explanation: That is about 2^28, the size of a hypothetical 28-bit search space, not this eight-bit model.

options.text: It cannot be brute-forced because the base changes after each crash
options.explanation: The prompt fixes the base. With independent uniform rerandomisation each time, success probability would instead be 1/256 per trial, with expectation 256; neither model supplies a duration.

questions.workedExample: There are 2^8 = 256 equiprobable candidates. For a fixed base and distinct guesses, the successful position is uniform from 1 to 256; its mean is 128.5. Independent uniform rerandomisation instead gives a geometric mean of 256 attempts. Request rate, restart costs and defences determine elapsed time, which is not given.

questions.prompt: A process has NX, ASLR and canaries. An out-of-bounds read reveals a pointer at a known offset in a known libc build. Why can that make another memory-corruption flaw more exploitable?

options.text: Because the leaked pointer contains the canary
options.explanation: A libc pointer is not the canary, though a different leak could reveal that.

options.text: It reveals the base and known offsets in that libc mapping
options.explanation: For that ordinary mapping, subtract the known offset to recover its base and locate other known offsets. This does not reveal every other mapping or disable NX/canaries.

options.text: Because out-of-bounds reads disable NX
options.explanation: A read does not change page permissions.

options.text: Because the read can be used to write memory
options.explanation: A read is a read. The danger is that it supplies the information a separate write bug needs.

questions.workedExample: For the known build and offset, `base = leaked_pointer - offset`. Other locations in that same mapping follow from their known offsets. A separate corruption flaw may make use of those addresses. The leak does not itself provide a write or guarantee a complete exploit.

questions.prompt: With a compatible GCC/glibc toolchain, a team adds `-D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3` to a debug build using `-O0`. Why are glibc’s fortified wrappers not enabled?

options.text: FORTIFY only checks heap buffers
options.explanation: It checks destinations whose size the compiler can determine, including local arrays.

options.text: FORTIFY needs optimisation (`-O1` or higher) to compute object sizes and swap in checked functions
options.explanation: Correct. Without optimisation, the fortified wrappers are not used. Enable it in optimised builds, where it is meant to run.

options.text: Level 3 is not a valid level
options.explanation: Level 3 is supported by compatible modern compiler/glibc combinations and uses dynamic object-size information. Support must be checked for the actual toolchain.

options.text: FORTIFY only checks `strcpy`, not `memcpy`
options.explanation: It covers a family of functions including `memcpy`, `memmove`, `strcpy`, `sprintf` and more.

questions.workedExample: `_FORTIFY_SOURCE` works through header magic: when the compiler can calculate the destination size (with `__builtin_object_size` or, at level 3, `__builtin_dynamic_object_size`), the call becomes `__memcpy_chk(dst, src, n, dst_size)`, which aborts if `n > dst_size`. That size analysis relies on the optimiser. At `-O0`, glibc does not enable the fortified wrappers (and recent versions warn). Run fortified checks in `-O2` builds, and use ASan in debug builds.

questions.prompt: For a conventional supported ELF toolchain using full RELRO (`-Wl,-z,relro,-z,now`), which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Required dynamic function bindings are resolved when the object is loaded instead of lazily on first call
options.explanation: `-z now` requests eager binding at program or shared-object load; it does not resolve every symbol in every future library before main.

options.text: After start-up, the GOT is made read-only
options.explanation: Correct. Once relocations are done the loader `mprotect`s the region, so an arbitrary write cannot redirect a library call through it.

options.text: Eager binding can increase work at load time relative to lazy binding
options.explanation: Work that lazy binding would defer is done earlier. Actual timing depends on the program and workload.

options.text: It prevents buffer overflows on the stack
options.explanation: RELRO protects one specific table of pointers; it does nothing about stack overflows.

questions.workedExample: Lazy function bindings need writable entries until resolution. Eager binding allows the loader to protect the designated relocation region, including the GOT in the conventional full-RELRO layout. Later object loads have their own relocation processing. This protects those entries, not every function pointer or buffer in the program.

questions.prompt: An attacker has bypassed ASLR with a leak and uses a stack overflow (with the canary also leaked) to chain together snippets of existing libc code, each ending in `ret`. Which mitigation is designed to stop exactly this?

options.text: DEP/NX
options.explanation: The snippets are in libc's executable code, so NX allows them. Code reuse exists precisely to get around NX.

options.text: A hardware shadow stack (for example Intel CET)
options.explanation: Correct. Each `ret` compares the return address on the normal stack with the protected copy on the shadow stack. The overwritten addresses don't match, so the first hijacked return faults.

options.text: Full RELRO
options.explanation: RELRO protects the GOT, not return addresses on the stack.

options.text: Using `-fstack-protector-strong` instead of `-fstack-protector`
options.explanation: The canary is already leaked and restored by the attacker; a stronger instrumentation policy does not help.

questions.workedExample:
1. The technique described is return-oriented programming: abusing `ret` instructions so that overwritten return addresses chain existing code snippets.
2. Its weak point is that it relies on *returns going somewhere other than where they were called from*.
3. A shadow stack stores a copy of each return address in memory that ordinary writes cannot modify. On `ret`, the CPU checks both copies match.
4. The first faked return fails the check. Forward-edge CFI (IBT, CFG) complements this for indirect calls and jumps.

questions.prompt: In a simplified MTE model, an eligible freed granule is retagged independently and uniformly over all 16 four-bit values. A stale pointer retains its old tag. What is the probability that this one tag comparison matches? Do not infer a real exploit success rate.

options.text: None; MTE always detects use-after-free
options.explanation: Tags are only 4 bits, so a reallocated chunk can by chance get the same tag as the stale pointer.

options.text: About 1 in 4 (25%)
options.explanation: This confuses the number of tag bits with the number of tag values; 4 bits give 16 values.

options.text: About 1 in 16 (6.25%)
options.explanation: Exactly one of 16 equally likely tags matches the old tag: 1/16 = 6.25%. This arithmetic does not establish how many real attempts crash or succeed.

options.text: About 1 in 65,536
options.explanation: That would need 16-bit tags. MTE stores 4 bits in the pointer's top byte.

questions.workedExample: Four bits represent 16 tags. Under the specified independent uniform model, one matches the stale tag, so P(match) = 1/16. Real allocator policies can exclude values or retag differently; unchecked accesses and same-granule overflows also affect protection. A mismatch report is immediate only in synchronous mode; asynchronous mode may report later.

questions.prompt: Which are **forward-edge** control-flow protections (guarding indirect calls and jumps) rather than backward-edge (returns)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Microsoft Control Flow Guard (CFG)
options.explanation: Correct. CFG checks indirect call targets against a bitmap of valid function starts.

options.text: Intel IBT (ENDBR64 landing pads)
options.explanation: With x86-64 IBT enabled, covered indirect branches must reach suitable ENDBR64 targets. Shadow stacks separately protect returns.

options.text: Clang `-fsanitize=cfi`
options.explanation: Clang provides indirect-call and virtual-call CFI schemes with type-based policies; their documented build requirements must be satisfied.

options.text: Intel CET shadow stack
options.explanation: This is the backward-edge half: it checks return addresses.

options.text: Stack canaries
options.explanation: Canaries are stack-corruption guards, not a general forward-edge CFI mechanism. They do not verify that each indirect call reaches a permitted target.

questions.workedExample: CFG, IBT/BTI and Clang forward-edge CFI constrain covered indirect transfers. A shadow stack checks returns against protected copies. A canary detects some stack corruption on protected exits and should not be treated as a complete return-integrity scheme. Enforcement and coverage must be enabled.

questions.prompt: The inspected glibc guard-initialization code clears the first byte in memory, which is the lowest byte on little-endian x86-64. How can this NUL byte hinder a conventional string-based overwrite or read?

options.text: To make it easier to compute
options.explanation: Generating the value is trivial either way; the zero byte has a security purpose.

options.text: A NUL-terminated copy cannot preserve that byte and continue past it, and a string read beginning before it stops there
options.explanation: An overflowing strcpy can overwrite the destination NUL, but cannot include that NUL in the source and then keep copying later bytes. A read starting after the zero can still disclose other guard bytes.

options.text: Because the CPU requires aligned values on the stack
options.explanation: Alignment concerns the address, not the value stored there.

options.text: To mark the end of the stack frame for debuggers
options.explanation: Debuggers use frame pointers or unwind tables, not the canary.

questions.workedExample: For a conventional forward copy, preserving the canary’s first zero byte requires a source NUL there, which ends the copy. The destination zero itself does not stop strcpy. A string read that reaches the intact zero stops, but a read starting after it can reveal remaining bytes. Length-based copying and other leaks remain relevant.
